summary: Evaluated 5 counter-evidenced claim clusters (out of brief.md's 9 sections; sections 1,2,6,8 and most of 7 were untargeted and stand as originally sourced). Stronger-original: 2 (parish-partnership pattern; calendar-timing-as-one-lever pattern, both survive minus their headline figures). Stronger-counter: 2 (calendar-timing causal attribution for the Feb 2024 spike is the most decisively won counter-argument in the set; referral LTV/trust claim is corrected and strengthened by counter-evidence's peer-reviewed sourcing). Mixed/no clear winner: 1 (authenticity-vs-production, contradicted by the brief's own best example on both sides, likely channel-dependent). Disproven/false as cited: 4 specific figures/framings -- the '30% user increase' figure (untraceable), the '83% higher trust' figure (misattributed Nielsen WOM stat), the 'calendar timing alone drove the spike' causal claim (confounded by a rare Ash-Wednesday/Super-Bowl coincidence, a celebrity ad, and 15x paid spend), and the unqualified 'authenticity beats production' blanket claim. Overstated-not-false: 'double-sided referral rewards are the dominant proven pattern' needs failure-mode caveats (abuse, cannibalization). Unresolved: whether Hallow/YouVersion tactics transfer to FellowScript's group/study-centric niche (correctly self-flagged in the original brief, confirmed still open by counter-evidence's honest null result), and whether authenticity or production wins for FellowScript specifically. All of the brief's directional recommendations survive; only specific statistics and blanket causal framings need correction before downstream use.
